competitors.name: Hilton Worldwide (HLT)
competitors.model: 97% franchised, 3% owned — most asset-light of the majors
competitors.strengths: Fastest franchise fee growth; highest franchise ratio; strong franchisee support; Hampton Inn proven profitability formula; digital key leadership
competitors.weaknesses: Limited luxury presence; heavy franchise reliance could dilute brand quality; smaller scale than MAR
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Primary rival. Hilton growing franchise fees faster (+5.57% vs +4.28%) but MAR's fee volume lead so large it would take Hilton ~40 years to catch up at current rates.

competitors.name: IHG Hotels & Resorts (IHG)
competitors.model: Asset-light, fee-driven. Strong in midscale (Holiday Inn) and growing luxury (Six Senses, Regent, InterContinental)
competitors.strengths: Strong global distribution (esp. Greater China); IHG One Rewards loyalty; Holiday Inn brand recognition; growing luxury portfolio
competitors.weaknesses: Smaller scale than MAR/HLT; luxury market share significantly behind MAR (8.8% vs 16.9%)
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Third-largest global chain. Strong in midscale/upper-midscale but trailing in luxury and total room count.

competitors.name: Hyatt Hotels (H)
competitors.model: Asset-light transition ongoing. Acquisitions (Apple Leisure Group, Mr & Mrs Smith) expanding lifestyle/luxury presence
competitors.strengths: Strong luxury positioning (#2 in luxury market share); World of Hyatt loyalty highly rated; lifestyle/experiential focus
competitors.weaknesses: Significantly smaller scale; narrower geographic footprint; higher owned/leased exposure historically
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Niche competitor focused on upper-upscale/luxury. Not a scale competitor but contests MAR in high-value luxury segment.

competitors.name: Accor
competitors.model: Complex structure with asset-light management/franchise plus some owned assets. Strongest in Europe and Middle East
competitors.strengths: Largest brand count; strong Europe/Middle East presence; Raffles/Fairmont/Sofitel luxury brands; ALL loyalty program
competitors.weaknesses: Complex corporate structure; weaker in North America; lower margins than US-focused peers
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Primarily a competitor in international markets, especially Europe and Middle East. Less direct competition in North America.

competitors.name: Wyndham Hotels & Resorts (WH)
competitors.strengths: Largest by property count in economy/midscale; high franchise ratio; Wyndham Rewards
competitors.weaknesses: Almost no luxury/upper-upscale presence; lower RevPAR and fee per room
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Competes on volume in economy/midscale tier. Minimal overlap with MAR's luxury/premium core.

competitors.name: Airbnb (ABNB)
competitors.notes: Disrupted hotel industry TAM by creating shared/alternative accommodations market. Not direct hotel competitor but captures leisure demand, especially in vacation/experiential travel segments.
competitors.competitive_dynamic: Indirect competitor. Expands total accommodation TAM but pressures midscale/economy hotels on price. Less impact on luxury/business segments where MAR is strongest.

competitive_dynamics: The global hotel industry in 2026 has shifted from post-pandemic recovery to a mature, rate-led growth environment. RevPAR growth is modest (+1-2%), driven by ADR rather than occupancy. Key competitive dynamics: (1) Brand proliferation/saturation — majors creating micro-brands to drive net unit growth; (2) Conversion vs. new-build — high construction costs and interest rates favor conversions; (3) Luxury outperformance — luxury RevPAR +6% while select-service flat, widening the quality premium; (4) Loyalty ecosystem wars — 270M+ Bonvoy members vs Hilton Honors ~190M, loyalty platforms increasingly central to direct booking and fee revenue; (5) Asset-light model convergence — all majors moving toward fee-driven models but with different franchise/management mixes; (6) Regional divergence — APAC/EMEA growing strongly while US/Canada flat; (7) AI/technology becoming table stakes for personalization, dynamic pricing, and distribution (agentic commerce).

moat_indicators.evidence: Largest room count globally (1.7M rooms). Scale drives purchasing power, operating efficiencies, and owner/franchisee value proposition. Hilton's fee growth is faster but would take ~40 years to close the gap.
31 brands across luxury/premium/select/extended-stay. Only competitor with comparable breadth is Accor (40+ but weaker execution). Captures travelers across every price point and occasion.
Bonvoy 270M+ members — largest hotel loyalty program. Co-branded credit card fees growing +33% in 2026. High switching costs for frequent travelers with status/points invested.
16.9% global luxury market share (#1), with Ritz-Carlton and St. Regis as iconic brands. Luxury RevPAR +6% outperforming other tiers — luxury moat widening.
~75% franchised + ~25% managed = capital-light, high-ROIC model. Operating margin 25% vs Hilton 22%. Minimal balance sheet risk from property ownership.

Hotel owners invest significant capital in brand-specific renovations, technology, and training. Long-term franchise agreements (typically 20+ years). Switching brands requires costly conversion. However, collection brands (Autograph, Tribute) lower entry barriers.
~610,000 rooms in pipeline (+6% YoY). Marriott leads in signed new construction rooms. Network effects: more rooms → more Bonvoy members → more bookings → more attractive to developers → more rooms.
Co-branded credit cards are a growing, high-margin revenue stream. Fee revenue from cards expected to rise by 33% in 2026 with new card launches. Creates financial moat layer beyond room fees.

industry_trends_2026.supply_growth: +1.4% US; record global pipeline of 2.4M rooms
industry_trends_2026.luxury_outperformance: Luxury RevPAR leading all tiers; luxury pipeline at record highs
industry_trends_2026.ai_technology: AI personalization shifting from differentiator to standard; agentic commerce reshaping distribution
industry_trends_2026.conversions: Record conversion activity due to high construction costs and interest rates
industry_trends_2026.regional_winners: APAC (Japan, Korea, Vietnam, India), Middle East, parts of EMEA
industry_trends_2026.regional_laggards: US select-service and extended-stay; government-related demand weak
industry_trends_2026.wellness_premium: Wellness travelers spend 40%+ above average; hotels with wellness report 20-35% higher ADR
industry_trends_2026.brand_saturation: Industry at or past brand saturation; micro-brands proliferating for net unit growth

dm_anchors.fact: MAR is #1 globally by room count (1.7M rooms, 9,361 properties). Hilton #2 (~1.18M rooms, 7,530 properties).
MAR has 31 brands vs Hilton 19 vs IHG 19 vs Accor 40+. MAR broadest in luxury-to-economy coverage among US peers.
Bonvoy 270M+ members (largest hotel loyalty program); +43M added in 2025; co-branded card fees +33% expected 2026
MAR luxury market share 16.9% (#1) vs Hyatt 11.4%, Accor 10%, IHG 8.8%; luxury RevPAR +6% in FY2025
MAR operating margin ~25% vs HLT ~22%; MAR ~75% franchised + ~25% managed vs HLT 97% franchised
Hotel franchise agreements typically 20+ years; brand-specific renovation requirements create high switching costs
MAR pipeline ~610K rooms (+6% YoY), leading in signed new construction rooms globally
Co-branded credit card fee revenue expected +33% in 2026 from new card launches
Global hotel pipeline Q4 2025: record 15,922 projects / 2,437,354 rooms; luxury pipeline +8% YoY
Global RevPAR forecast +1-2% for 2026, rate-led; occupancy flat in high 50s to low 60s
Hilton franchise/licensing fee growth 5.57% annually vs MAR 4.28%; but MAR volume lead requires ~40 years for HLT to close
Wellness travelers spend 40%+ above average per trip; hotels with integrated wellness report 20-35% higher ADR
US & China together account for ~62% of global hotel pipeline projects
